```{python}
INK = "#1B1B19"
plt.rcParams.update({
    "figure.facecolor": "white", "axes.facecolor": "white", "savefig.facecolor": "white",
    "text.color": INK, "axes.edgecolor": INK, "axes.labelcolor": INK,
    "xtick.color": INK, "ytick.color": INK, "axes.spines.top": False,
    "axes.spines.right": False, "axes.linewidth": 0.6, "font.size": 10,
    "legend.frameon": False, "lines.color": INK, "axes.prop_cycle": plt.cycler(color=[INK]),
})
STYLES = ["-", "--", ":", "-.", (0, (5, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1))]
SEEDS = np.arange(1, 501)
defaults = Params()
net = defaults.with_(turn_endowment=1.0)
eq = equilibrium(defaults)
table = lambda df, **kw: Markdown(df.to_markdown(index=False, **kw))
```

## Summary

This is a rebuild of an agent-based model I wrote in NetLogo in 2020. Sixty players are
paired at random each turn. One of each pair, the proposer, claims a share of the other's
money. The responder either pays, or destroys everything they own so that the proposer gets
nothing. A proposer whose claim is accepted grows greedier; one who is rejected feels shame
and asks for less next time.

```{python}
#| echo: false
h_default = run(defaults, SEEDS)
h_net = run(net.with_(turns=400), SEEDS[:200])
lr = long_run(h_net)
Markdown(f"""
- **The first turn is a massacre.** With the original settings every responder rejects, and
  {h_default.rejected[0].mean():.0f} of 60 players lose everything at once. The proposers who
  caused it lose nothing.
- **Claims never settle. They saw.** A take rate creeps up by {defaults.greed:.0%} per accepted
  claim until it is rejected, then drops by {defaults.shame:.0%}. It is the pattern of TCP
  congestion control.
- **The rejection rate is set by shame and greed alone:**
  $\\log(1+g) / (\\log(1+g) - \\log(1-s))$. For the original settings that is
  {eq.rejection_rate:.1%}; simulation gives {lr['rejection_rate']:.1%}. How tolerant responders
  are does not enter.
- **Shame protects responders twice.** Fewer are ruined, and the average claim
  ({lr['mean_claim']:.0%}) sits well below what they would tolerate ({defaults.tolerance_mean:.0%}).
- **Without a safety net the game dies.** A ruined player earns no interest and never returns.
  After 100 turns {h_default.broke[-1].mean():.0f} of 60 cannot play and the Gini coefficient
  is {h_default.gini[-1].mean():.2f}. A payment of 1 per turn keeps everyone in.
""")
```

The [web page](../) runs the same model in the browser.

## The game

The model is a *power-to-take* game rather than a textbook ultimatum game. In the ultimatum
game a proposer offers a split of their own windfall. Here the proposer takes from the
responder's money, and the responder's only weapon is to burn their own wealth. The setup
follows the experiment of
[Reuben and van Winden (2010)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joep.2010.08.001), who found that
proposers who had taken what they themselves thought unfair felt shame and guilt after being
punished, and lowered their claims. The model takes that one mechanism and repeats it across
a population.

**Each turn:**

1. Players are shuffled. Half become responders, half proposers, and they are paired off.
2. A pair plays if the responder has any money and the proposer has at least `cost_to_play`.
3. The proposer claims their *take rate* times the responder's money.
4. If the take rate is at most the responder's *tolerance*, the money moves and the proposer's
   take rate is multiplied by `1 + greed` (capped at 1). Otherwise the responder's money is
   destroyed and the proposer's take rate is multiplied by `1 - shame`.
5. Everyone earns `interest` on what they hold, then receives `turn_endowment`.

```{python}
#| echo: false
rows = [
    ("players", defaults.players, "Number of players"),
    ("take_mean, take_sd", f"{defaults.take_mean}, {defaults.take_sd}", "Starting take rates (normal)"),
    ("tolerance_mean, tolerance_sd", f"{defaults.tolerance_mean}, {defaults.tolerance_sd}", "Largest take rate a responder accepts (normal, fixed for life)"),
    ("shame", defaults.shame, "Cut in take rate after a rejection"),
    ("greed", defaults.greed, "Rise in take rate after an acceptance"),
    ("endowment", f"normal({defaults.endowment_mean:g}, {defaults.endowment_sd:g})", "Starting money"),
    ("interest", defaults.interest, "Interest per turn"),
    ("turn_endowment", defaults.turn_endowment, "Paid to every player each turn"),
    ("cost_to_play", defaults.cost_to_play, "Money a proposer needs in order to propose"),
]
table(pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["Parameter", "Default", "Meaning"]))
```

The defaults are the settings saved in the 2020 NetLogo file.

### What changed from the NetLogo version

| 2020 model | This version | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Responders linked to whichever players stood on neighbouring patches | Each responder is paired with exactly one proposer | In the original a responder could face several proposers, or none, or another responder. Transfers were then paid to every linked player, so money was created |
| Stopped as soon as one turn had no games | Runs a fixed number of turns | Keeps runs comparable; idle turns are recorded as such |
| Called an ultimatum game | Described as a power-to-take game | That is the game the rules implement |
| Explored by moving sliders | Closed-form predictions, tested against simulation | The interesting behaviour has an exact explanation |

The README of the original said rejected proposers lose their money. The code destroyed the
responder's, which is also what the power-to-take game specifies, and that is what is kept.

## The first turn

Proposers start at a take rate of about 80%; responders tolerate about 50%. Nobody has learned
anything yet, so every claim is rejected.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Responders ruined in the first turn, out of 30, by the take rate proposers start with."
ft = pd.DataFrame(first_turn())
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(ft.take_mean, ft.ruined, marker="s", ms=4, lw=1)
ax.axvline(defaults.tolerance_mean, ls=":", lw=0.8)
ax.text(defaults.tolerance_mean + 0.008, 1, "mean tolerance", fontsize=8)
ax.set(xlabel="Starting take rate", ylabel="Responders ruined", ylim=(0, 31))
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}")
plt.show()
```

The cost of this lesson falls entirely on the responders. A rejected proposer keeps their
money and comes back claiming $0.8 \times (1 - 0.6) = 0.32$.

## The sawtooth

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Take rate of four proposers over 150 turns (with a per-turn payment so that everyone keeps playing). Dotted line: mean tolerance."
params = net.with_(turns=150)
seed = np.array([7])
pop = initial_population(params, seed)
trace = []
for t in range(params.turns):
    step(pop, params, seed, t)
    trace.append(pop.take[0, :4].copy())
trace = np.array(trace)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for i in range(4):
    ax.plot(trace[:, i], lw=0.9, ls=STYLES[i])
ax.axhline(params.tolerance_mean, ls=":", lw=0.8)
ax.set(xlabel="Turn", ylabel="Take rate", ylim=(0, 1))
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}")
plt.show()
```

After the first shock each proposer climbs by 5% per accepted claim, crosses some responder's
tolerance, and falls by 60%. Flat stretches are turns spent as a responder or without a game.
Multiplicative increase with multiplicative decrease is the scheme TCP uses to probe the
capacity of a network link, and it gives the same sawtooth.

### The rejection-rate law

Write $x = \log(\text{take rate})$. Each time a proposer plays, $x$ rises by
$L_g = \log(1 + g)$ if accepted and falls by $L_s = -\log(1 - s)$ if rejected. The take rate
is confined to $(0, 1]$, so over a long run the rises and falls must cancel. If a share $r$ of
a proposer's claims are rejected,

$$(1 - r)\,L_g = r\,L_s \quad\Longrightarrow\quad r = \frac{L_g}{L_g + L_s} = \frac{\log(1+g)}{\log(1+g) - \log(1-s)}$$

Nothing about the responders appears. Their tolerance fixes the height at which the walk
turns round, not how often it turns. Equivalently, one rejection takes $L_s / L_g$ accepted
claims to undo: `{python} f"{-np.log1p(-defaults.shame) / np.log1p(defaults.greed):.1f}"` with
the default settings.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Long-run rejection rate. Lines: the formula. Squares: simulation, 200 worlds of 400 turns, first 150 discarded."
law = pd.DataFrame(law_grid())
s = np.linspace(0.02, 0.98, 200)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for style, (g, grp) in zip(STYLES, law.groupby("greed")):
    ax.plot(s, rejection_rate(s, g), ls=style, lw=1, label=f"greed {g:.0%}")
    ax.plot(grp.shame, grp.rejection_rate, "s", ms=3.5)
ax.set(xlabel="Shame", ylabel="Share of claims rejected", ylim=(0, 1))
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}")
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}")
ax.legend()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
err = (law.rejection_rate - law.predicted_rejection_rate).abs()
tol = [long_run(run(net.with_(tolerance_mean=m, turns=400), SEEDS[:200]))["rejection_rate"] for m in (0.2, 0.5, 0.8)]
Markdown(f"Across the {len(law)} settings the largest gap between formula and simulation is "
         f"{err.max():.4f} (mean {err.mean():.4f}). Moving the mean tolerance from 20% to 50% to 80% "
         f"gives rejection rates of {tol[0]:.3f}, {tol[1]:.3f} and {tol[2]:.3f}: no effect, as predicted.")
```

### How much is taken

When responders' tolerances are close together, a proposer's take rate cycles between a
ceiling $c$ (about the mean tolerance) and a floor $c(1 - s)$, spending equal time in equal
steps of $\log$ take rate. Averaging over a cycle,

$$\text{average take} \approx c \cdot \frac{s}{-\log(1 - s)}$$

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Average claim as a share of what responders tolerate. Line: the sawtooth approximation. Markers: simulation at each level of greed."
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(s, mean_take_fraction(s), lw=1)
for marker, (g, grp) in zip("s^ovD", law.groupby("greed")):
    ax.plot(grp.shame, grp.mean_claim / defaults.tolerance_mean, marker, ms=4, mfc="white", label=f"greed {g:.0%}")
ax.set(xlabel="Shame", ylabel="Average claim / tolerance", ylim=(0, 1.1))
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}")
ax.legend()
plt.show()
```

The approximation is good when greed is small and runs low when greed is large, because a
proposer who climbs in big steps overshoots the ceiling before being stopped. It is an
approximation; the rejection-rate law is exact.

Together the two results describe a trade-off that shame controls. Little shame means claims
stay near the limit and a large share of them end in ruin. Much shame means rejections are
rare and proposers spend most of their time asking for far less than they could get.

## Ruin and the safety net

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Players unable to propose (left) and Gini coefficient of wealth (right). Mean of 500 worlds, with the 10th to 90th percentile shaded."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 3.6))
turns = np.arange(1, defaults.turns + 1)
h_one = run(net, SEEDS)
for ax, key, label in zip(axes, ("broke", "gini"), ("Players broke", "Gini coefficient")):
    for h, style, name in ((h_default, "-", "no payment"), (h_one, "--", "1 per turn")):
        v = getattr(h, key)
        ax.fill_between(turns, *np.percentile(v, [10, 90], axis=1), color=INK, alpha=0.12, lw=0)
        ax.plot(turns, v.mean(axis=1), ls=style, lw=1, label=name)
    ax.set(xlabel="Turn", ylabel=label)
axes[0].legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

With no per-turn payment, interest on nothing is nothing: a player who destroys their money
is out for good, and because they cannot propose they also never learn. Each rejection removes
one more player. The survivors are the first turn's proposers, who collect interest and each
other's money while the number of games falls towards zero.

```{python}
#| echo: false
sn = pd.DataFrame(safety_net())
table(sn[["turn_endowment", "broke_at_end", "games_per_turn", "gini_at_end"]].rename(columns={
    "turn_endowment": "Paid per turn", "broke_at_end": "Players broke at turn 100",
    "games_per_turn": "Games per turn (of 30)", "gini_at_end": "Gini at turn 100"}), floatfmt=".2f")
```

A small payment is enough to keep the society playing. It has a cost the table does not show:
ruined players return with the take rate they started with, never having been shamed, and
their first claim ruins someone else. With a safety net the lesson of the first turn is
re-taught for many turns before the population has learned it.

## Limitations

- **Responders never learn.** Tolerance is fixed for life. A responder who has burned their
  money might reasonably tolerate more next time; the model does not allow it.
- **One number per emotion.** Shame and greed are the same for everyone and do not depend on
  how unfair the claim was. Reuben and van Winden's point was precisely that fairness
  perceptions differ.
- **Destruction is all or nothing.** In the experiments responders could destroy part of
  their income.
- **The predictions assume everyone keeps playing.** They hold with a per-turn payment and
  fail without one, as shown above.
- **Interest makes wealth grow without bound,** so totals are not meaningful across long runs.
  Shares and the Gini coefficient are.
- It is a toy. It shows what these rules imply, not how people behave.

## Reproducing this

```sh
uv sync --group report
uv run pytest                      # the model and the theory
uv run ultimatum-abm build         # experiments and browser fixtures
npm test                           # the browser engine, checked against Python
quarto render report/index.qmd
```

Random numbers come from a counter-based generator (`ultimatum_abm/rng.py`) built from 32-bit
integer operations, so a seed gives the same world in NumPy and in JavaScript. A test replays
trajectories exported from Python through the browser engine and requires exact equality.
